name: Jurchens
info: The Jurchens were Tungusic-speaking peoples of Manchuria, first recorded in 748, who founded the Jin dynasty (1115–1234) and, under Nurhaci, the Later Jin, before Hong Taiji renamed them Manchus in 1635.

facts.homeland: the forests and river valleys of Manchuria, in what is now China's Heilongjiang and Jilin provinces and Russia's Primorsky Krai; the Mudan River, the Changbai mountains, Liaodong, the Songhua and Amur rivers and the Yalu and Tumen borderlands
facts.period: first in Chinese records in 748; vassals of the Liao dynasty by the 11th century; the Wanyan federation under Wugunai (1021–74); the Jin dynasty (1115–1234); Jianzhou, Haixi and Wild Jurchens under the Ming dynasty (1368–1644); unification under Nurhaci from 1586; renamed Manchus in 1635
facts.known: the Jin dynasty and the capture of Kaifeng in 1127; the Jurchen script of 1120; the Eight Banners; the queue hairstyle; horsemanship, archery and hunting; trade in pearls and ginseng; founding the Qing dynasty
facts.sources: Chinese records from 748, the History of Jin and the Ming Veritable Records; Korean accounts such as that of the emissary Sin Chung-il in 1595; the Yongning Temple steles at Telin in four languages; oral tradition of the Wanyan clan; a burial ground excavated by Russian archaeologists in Primorye in 2012; genetic studies of the Aisin Gioro

t: The Jurchens were culturally diverse: some groups lived as hunter-gatherers, some as semi-nomadic pastoralists and most as sedentary farmers.
Wanyan Aguda unified the Jurchen tribes in 1115 and founded the Jin dynasty, which conquered the Liao in 1125 and took the Song capital of Kaifeng in 1127 before falling to the Mongols in 1234.
Nurhaci, a Jianzhou chieftain, united the Jurchen tribes from 1586 and organised them into the Eight Banners, and his son Hong Taiji renamed the people Manchus in 1635.
dyk: The Jin dynasty's name means "gold" and comes from the "Gold River", Aisin in Manchu, in the Jurchens' ancestral homeland.
ev: The Jurchens first appear in Chinese records
Goryeo sends 170,000 soldiers against the Jurchens and builds the Nine Fortresses, later handed back
Wanyan Aguda unifies the Jurchen tribes and declares himself emperor of the Jin
Wanyan Xiyin invents the Jurchen script on Aguda's orders
The Jin capture the Song capital of Kaifeng in the Jingkang incident
Caizhou falls to the Mongols, ending the Jin dynasty
The Ming create the Nurgan Command Post at Telin on the lower Amur
Hong Taiji renames the Jurchens as Manchus

sections.origins:
When the Jurchens first entered Chinese records in 748, they lived in the forests and river valleys of what is now divided between China's Heilongjiang Province and Russia's Primorsky Krai. Earlier records name this land as the home of the Sushen, the Yilou, the Wuji and the Mohe. Scholarship since the Qing period has traced the Jurchens to the Wanyan tribe of the Mohe or to the Heishui or Blackwater Mohe, but continuity with these earlier peoples remains conjectural. The Mohe, their tentative ancestors, were people of the multi-ethnic kingdom of Balhae: mainly sedentary farmers who grew soybean, wheat, millet and rice, kept pigs and rode reindeer.

There is no dated evidence of the Jurchens before the time of Wugunai (1021–74), when they began to coalesce into a nation-like federation. Oral tradition made him the sixth-generation descendant of Hanpu, founder of the Wanyan clan, who came from the Heishui Mohe of Balhae by way of Goryeo. Herbert Franke called this story an "ancestral legend" reflecting the clan's absorption of immigrants from Goryeo and Balhae in the 10th century. The later Qing emperor Hong Taiji told another legend, of a heavenly maiden who became pregnant after eating a red fruit dropped by a magpie.

The name Jurchen is a reconstruction of an unattested native form, transcribed in Khitan as Julisen; Chinese wrote it Nüzhen and Nüzhi. Vajda considers that it probably derives from Tungusic words for "reindeer people".
sections.society:
Most Jurchens were sedentary farmers. They grew grain and millet as their main cereals, grew flax and raised oxen, pigs, sheep and horses; "at the most" they could be called semi-nomadic. Ming officials divided them into three groups. The Jianzhou Jurchens, near the Mudan River, the Changbai mountains and Liaodong, hunted and fished, farmed and traded in pearls and ginseng, and were said to make clothes like the Chinese. The Haixi Jurchens of the Songhua River were semi-nomadic pastoralists in the west and farmers in the east. The Yeren, or Wild Jurchens, of the sparse north lived by hunting, fishing, pig farming and some migratory agriculture.

Like the Khitans and Mongols, they prized strength, horsemanship, archery and hunting, and they did not observe primogeniture: any capable son or nephew could be chosen as leader. A powerful chief was called beile. In the cold north-east they sometimes sank their brick or timber houses half into the ground and surrounded fortified villages with wattle and mud walls on stone foundations, and village clusters were ruled by hereditary beile.

Under the Ming they lived in sub-clans (mukun) of ancient clans (hala), whose members were not all related by blood. A household (boo) was a family of five to seven kin and a number of slaves. Households formed squads (tatan) for hunting and gathering and companies (niru) for war. Abduction marriages were common, and marriage with in-laws was allowed. Under the Jin, poor Jurchen families in the south sold daughters into slavery and rented land to Han tenants, which Emperor Shizong tried to halt in 1181.
sections.beliefs:
The Jurchens practised shamanic rituals and believed in a supreme sky goddess, abka hehe, literally "sky woman". Their word for a sorceress was shanman. Under the Jin dynasty Buddhism became the prevalent religion of the Jurchens, alongside Taoism. Much later, under Confucian influence during the Qing dynasty, the sky goddess became a male sky father, Abka Enduri.

Their own traditions of origin were sacred stories. The Wanyan clan remembered its founder Hanpu as a "wise man" who settled a feud between two families without violence. The Aisin Gioro clan of the Qing told of three heavenly maidens bathing at Bulhūri Omo, one of whom conceived the ancestor Bukūri Yongšon from a red fruit. An older and simpler version recorded in 1635 from Muksike of the Hurha tribe placed the lake near the Amur river instead of the Changbai Mountains.

Around the time of the Ming dynasty the Jurchens began to revere dogs, though their Mohe ancestors had not, and passed this on to the Manchus. It was forbidden to harm, kill or eat a dog or to use dog skin. Until recently little was known of their burials. In July 2012 Russian archaeologists found a Jurchen burial ground in Partizansky District of Primorye: fifteen graves of the 12th or 13th century, a chieftain's in the centre with those of 14 servants around it, all holding pots of ashes, which shows the Jurchens cremated their dead. The chieftain's grave held a quiver of arrows and a bent sword, perhaps bent to show he would no longer need it.
sections.arts:
The early Jurchen script was invented in 1120 by Wanyan Xiyin on the orders of Wanyan Aguda. It was based on the Khitan script, which had in turn been inspired by Chinese characters. Written Jurchen died out soon after the fall of the Jin dynasty: in 1444 the Jurchens told the Ming Translators' Bureau that nobody among them understood the script, and asked for letters in Mongolian. Until the end of the 16th century they used a mix of Mongolian and Chinese, until Nurhaci patronised an alphabet based on the Mongolian script and Manchu became the new literary language. Wilhelm Grube did the pioneering study of the Jurchen script at the end of the 19th century.

A Ming account described the people of Jianzhou and Maolian as skilled in spinning and weaving, with food, clothing and utensils like those of the Chinese. The Korean emissary Sin Chung-il, who visited Nurhaci's followers at Fe Ala in 1595, saw that all wore the same dress and hairstyle: the front of the scalp shaved and the rest in a long plaited braid, with leather boots, breeches and tunics. In midwinter he watched them dance, wrestle and drink strong liquor.

The steles that the Ming envoy Yishiha raised at the Yongning Temple at Telin near the mouth of the Amur, a Guanyin temple he built in 1413, carry inscriptions in Chinese, Jurchen, Mongol and Tibetan. The Jurchens and their Manchu descendants also used Khitan elements, such as suffixes, in their personal names.
sections.exchange:
By the 11th century the Jurchens were vassals of the Khitan Liao dynasty, while those of the Yalu River had been tributaries of Goryeo since Taejo (r. 918-943), who used Jurchen cavalry against Later Baekje. They paid tribute to both courts and switched allegiance as it suited them, and those who brought tribute were often the same who raided the border. In 1019 Jurchen pirates raided Japan for slaves, killing 374 people and taking 1,280 prisoner. Under Wuyashu (r. 1103–1113) the Wanyan clan broke the clans' allegiance to Goryeo; Goryeo's army of 170,000 built the Nine Fortresses in 1107, but they were handed back. One cause of the revolt against the Liao was the Khitan practice of forcing married Jurchen women to provide sexual services to Khitan envoys.

Aguda founded the Jin in 1115, seized the Liao northern capital in 1120, conquered the Liao in 1125 and in the Jin–Song Wars overran most of northern China, taking Kaifeng in 1127. In 1126 the Jin ordered Han men to shave their heads in the Jurchen manner, then lifted the order. From 1189 the Jin fought the Mongols; they moved their capital from Zhongdu to Kaifeng in 1215, and Kaifeng fell in 1233 and Caizhou in 1234.

The Ming made allies of the Jurchens against the Mongols, setting up 178 commanderies under hereditary leaders and, in 1409, the Nurgan Command Post at Telin, abolished in 1434. Joseon contested control of them. In the ninth year of the Xuande Emperor famine forced Jurchens under Ming rule to sell their daughters and seek relief in Liaodong. From 1586 Nurhaci united the tribes.
sections.legacy:
Over thirty years from 1586 Nurhaci, a chieftain of the Jianzhou Jurchens, united most of the Jurchen tribes, enrolled the whole population in the hereditary regiments of the Eight Banners and founded the Later Jin, with himself as ruler (r. 1616–26). In 1635 his son and successor Hong Taiji decreed that Manchu was to be the only acceptable name for his people, as a clear break from their past as Chinese vassals, and called the old name jušen demeaning. In Manchu the word came to describe serfs, though not slaves, of the free Manchus. The dynasty became the Qing (1636–1912), and the Manchus, like the Jin before them, made Han men shave the front of their heads and wear the queue.

The Qing rewrote the record of their origins. The History of Ming left out the Ming Veritable Records on the Jurchens to hide their former subservience, and the original editions of two Qing chronicles were kept from public view because they showed the Aisin Gioro family ruled by the Ming.

Not all the Jurchens became Manchus. Many of the peoples once called Yeren Jurchens, such as the Nivkh, Negidai, Nanai, Oroqen and many Evenks, are today considered distinct ethnic groups, and in Outer Manchuria the descendants of Han men and local women became the Taz people. Genetic studies of men claiming Aisin Gioro descent trace that clan's paternal line to the middle Amur and to ancestors related to the Daurs. The Jurchens also appear in fiction and in the video games Age of Empires II and Age of Empires IV.

summary: The Jurchens were Tungusic-speaking hunters, herders and farmers of Manchuria, long tributaries of the Liao, Goryeo and the Ming. Twice they built conquest dynasties in China: the Jin of Wanyan Aguda, which took northern China and fell to the Mongols in 1234, and the Later Jin of Nurhaci, whose people Hong Taiji renamed Manchus in 1635 before they founded the Qing.
